source: McCauley et al. (2008) Debugging: a review of the literature from an educational perspective (extracts)
finding: Review says some, but not most, novice breakdowns come from misconceptions about language constructs. Most errors come from chains of cognitive breakdowns in skill, rule or knowledge.
numbers: No counts. Rule breakdowns: wrong or bad rule, often from fragile knowledge. Knowledge breakdowns: fragile knowledge and the superbug.
quote: root causes of bugs stem from preconceptions, misconceptions, and the fragility of knowledge
limits: I opened a course handout of extracts, not the full paper.
agent_relevance: Misconceptions are one cause of bugs among several. Keep a plan/rule-slip branch next to the false-belief branch.

source: McCauley et al. (2008) review extracts: bug types and the superbug
finding: Most novice bugs are missing or malformed code. Some are endemic across languages: off-by-one, operator precedence, code placed in or out of a loop. The superbug is the belief that the language has a hidden intelligence.
numbers: Finding bugs quickly depends on large-scale program comprehension, not small chunks. Superbug defined on p71.
quote: belief that there is a hidden mind somewhere in the programming language that has intelligent interpretive powers
limits: Extract only.
agent_relevance: LLM agents can show an analogue of the superbug: assuming the tool or the reader will infer what was meant. Add a check for what was assumed.

source: Michaeli & Romeike (2019) Improving debugging skills in the classroom: effects of teaching a systematic debugging process
finding: A 10 minute lesson on a systematic debugging process raised debugging self-efficacy and bugs fixed in year 10 pupils compared with a control class that only practised debugging.
numbers: Experimental class n=13, control n=15, same teacher, BlueJ/Java, pre-post with control. Self-efficacy rose significantly in pilot (n=14, d=0.56) and experimental (d=0.54) groups, not in control. Post-test bugs fixed: experimental median 4 of 9, control median 2 (Mann-Whitney p=0.049). Pre-test difference p=0.191.
quote: Debugging is distinct from general programming abilities, therefore it should be taught explicitly
limits: Small samples, no random assignment, one school and teacher. Post-test used harder tasks than pre-test. Number of bugs was told to pupils. Actual process use not observed.
agent_relevance: A short explicit process beats unguided practice. Supports a schema state that names the debugging steps.

source: Michaeli & Romeike (2019) related work: teaching debugging processes
finding: Earlier studies: students kept using whichever process they were taught first (Katz & Anderson, LISP). Written debugging notes raised bugs fixed but not bugs found (Allwood & Bjorhag). Few students kept using a taught Wolf Fence procedure (Boettcher et al).
numbers: Chmiel & Loui: voluntary debugging tasks cut debugging time but exam scores were only slightly better. Carver & Risinger: one hour of LOGO training shifted brute force to systematic use (no control).
quote: only a few students applied the conveyed systematic process, but quickly returned to a non-systematic
limits: Secondhand report of older studies; I did not open them.
agent_relevance: Telling a process is not enough; use decays under load. The scaffold should enforce the steps.

source: Michaeli & Romeike (2019) classroom observation on error classes
finding: Pupils were not aware of different classes of errors even though they met them often. Only explicit reflection on their own errors made them notice.
numbers: Qualitative remark; no counts given.
limits: Observation, not a measured outcome.
agent_relevance: Ask the agent to classify an error (syntax, semantic, logic) before fixing it.

source: Hellas et al. (2023) Exploring the responses of LLMs to beginner programmers' help requests
finding: GPT-3.5 found at least one real issue in 90 percent of 150 student help requests but all issues in only 57 percent, and added false issues in 40 percent.
numbers: 4,247 students, 831 help requests in 2022; 150 sampled (10 per each of 15 exercises), 275 issues, mean 1.9 per request. GPT-3.5: 123 of 150 found one issue, 82 found all, 72 requests had a non-existing issue. Codex about 70 percent in English. Conditionals fully addressed 35 percent, iteration 73 percent.
limits: Codex and GPT-3.5 only, one course, one year. LLMs gave code even when told not to. Finnish prompts only slightly worse.
agent_relevance: Weak models miss co-occurring faults and invent faults. List all candidate faults and test each against evidence.

source: Hellas et al. (2023) help-request issue types
finding: Real novice help requests were mostly logic errors, not syntax.
numbers: Logic 108 requests (72 percent), input/output 51 (34 percent), syntax 12 (8.0 percent), very incomplete solutions 8 (5.3 percent), semicolons 4 (2.7 percent), hidden test requirements 3 (2.0 percent).
limits: Single course; first-pass annotation by one researcher.
agent_relevance: Benchmarks heavy on syntax errors misrepresent the real novice distribution.

source: Leinonen et al. (2022) Using LLMs to enhance programming error messages
finding: Codex gave an explanation of a Python error in 67 to 100 percent of cases, but the explanation was often wrong and its fix was correct only 33 percent of the time.
numbers: Correct explanation 11 percent (unexpected EOF while parsing) to 83 percent (can't assign to function call). Fix offered in 44 to 89 percent of cases, correct 33 percent overall (17 to 56 percent). Better than the original message in 54 percent of cases (22 to 78 percent). Empty responses across five prompts: 4, 6, 7, 16, 27 of 81.
limits: Codex-era model, two raters, one language, small message set.
agent_relevance: Confident explanations can be wrong. Run the fix before trusting it.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Studying the effect of AI code generators on novice learners (CHI)
finding: Novices with Codex did better in training and no worse on later tests without it. One week later they were slightly but not significantly better.
numbers: 69 finished (33 Codex, 36 baseline) of 90, 45 tasks over 10 sessions in 3 weeks, matched on Scratch pre-test (62.7 vs 60 percent). Training correctness d=1.67, time d=1.56, errors 0.59x. Immediate post-test authoring 61.3 vs 62.9 percent (d=0.05), modifying d=0.01. Retention: Codex 12.7 percent higher on modifying, not significant.
limits: 21 of 90 dropped out. Short horizon, bootcamp volunteers, Codex model. Learners with more prior skill gained more.
agent_relevance: AI help raises success without hurting novices on average, but the benefit depends on prior skill.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) How novices use LLM-based code generators (log analysis)
finding: Of 1,666 Codex requests, 52 percent of prompts were copied from the task text. Heavy single-prompt use trended negative for later scores and hybrid use trended positive.
numbers: By task: AI Single Prompt 46 percent (628), Manual 29 percent (398), Hybrid 19 percent (252), AI Step-by-Step 6 percent (82). 81 percent of generated code was high quality. AI code was tested in 60 percent of uses. 57 tasks used Codex only to debug.
limits: Trends were not significant; correlational; Codex only.
agent_relevance: Mixing own work with AI beat delegating everything. Keep a verify-by-running step.

source: Prather et al. (2023) Usability and interactions with Copilot for novice programmers
finding: Observed novices with Copilot. Two patterns: shepherding (retyping suggestions) and drifting (adapting wrong generated code deeper into a debugging rabbit hole).
numbers: 30 minute Minesweeper task in C++. 13 participants deleted just-accepted code at least once.
limits: Qualitative, small sample, early Copilot version.
agent_relevance: Add a stop rule: if repeated edits of generated code do not improve test results, discard it and restate the problem.

source: Prather et al. (2024) The widening gap: benefits and harms of GenAI for novice programmers
finding: In a replication of a no-AI lab study, strong students accelerated with GenAI. Struggling students kept old metacognitive difficulties, gained new ones, and showed an illusion of competence.
numbers: 21 students, 20 finished. Time 5 to 35 min, mean 17.1 (SD 8.1). Copilot acceptance 10 to 53 percent. Time vs metacognitive difficulties r=0.693 (p=0.0005). Grade vs time r=-0.727. Grade vs new difficulties r=-0.503 (p=0.020). Self-efficacy vs grade r=0.553. Original study had n=31 and five difficulties; three new ones added.
limits: N=21, one class, many correlations without correction, one problem.
agent_relevance: AI amplifies existing skill gaps. An agent without self-monitoring gains confidence, not correctness.

source: Ma et al. (2024) HypoCompass: LLMs as teachable agents for debugging
finding: Novices acted as teaching assistants to LLM agents and practised hypothesising bug causes. Score rose 11.7 percent and time fell 13.6 percent pre to post.
numbers: 19 students, four US institutions. Paired t-test score p=0.033, time p=0.003. Self-rated debugging confidence up 15 percent (Wilcoxon p=0.007). Material generation 90 percent success on 145 buggy programs, six problems, four times faster than humans.
limits: No control group, N=19, one-hour session; gains may be practice effects.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis writing is the skill worth training. Matches our explicit-hypothesis states.

source: Al-Hossami et al. (2024) Can language models employ the Socratic method? Experiments with code debugging
finding: On a Socratic debugging benchmark GPT-4 beat GPT-3.5. Chain-of-thought prompting made GPT-4 output worse in manual review.
numbers: 149 instructor utterances in 43 turns over 11 dialogues reviewed. GPT-4 made 32 good utterances not in the dataset vs 10 for GPT-3.5, and 42 poor vs over 96. False positives 41 vs 93.
limits: Small manual sample. Overlap metrics did not track quality for CoT output.
agent_relevance: More reasoning text is not always better for tutoring dialogue.

source: Al-Hossami & Bunescu (2025) McMining: automated discovery of misconceptions in student code
finding: LLMs can name the false belief behind student code. Best multi-sample setup reached 82.0 percent accuracy, best single-sample 78.5 percent.
numbers: 1,063 code samples, 67 misconceptions. Multi-instance 82.0 percent (Claude Sonnet 4.5 with reasoning). On bags with a misconception 93.3 percent, on correct-only bags 59.3 percent. Syntax confusions such as = vs == above 95 percent; subtle benign cases lower (48 percent on one out-of-distribution case). 41 novel true positives (12.1 percent of bags).
limits: Part of the code was LLM-generated with injected misconceptions. High false positive rate on clean code.
agent_relevance: Misconception naming is feasible, but needs a no-fault option to avoid over-diagnosis.

source: Al-Hossami & Bunescu (2026) Reasoning trajectories for Socratic debugging
finding: Frames Socratic debugging as a chain of steps ending in a statement that contradicts the student's misconception. LLM judges rated up to 91 percent of trajectories correct and 98.7 percent of turns valid.
numbers: 501 problems, 558 solutions, 40 misconceptions; 227 triplets built. GPT-5 trajectory validity 85 to 91 percent across 14 LLM configurations. Judge agreement 96.6 percent on 88 teacher utterances.
limits: LLM-as-judge validated on 30 trajectories. Synthetic bugs. No student learning outcome measured.
agent_relevance: Contradiction-seeking: find an observed fact that conflicts with the current belief. Fits a falsification operator.

source: Golrang et al. (2026) Not all scaffolds are equal: initiation mode and EMME in debugging
finding: Eye-movement modelling examples raised novice debugging scores over control. Teacher- or learner-started help beat automated triggering. EMME removed the advantage of prior knowledge.
numbers: 120 undergraduates, four groups, ten Python tasks. One-way ANOVA F(3,116)=132.44. T-EMME M=6.56 (SD 1.16), L-EMME M=6.93 (SD 0.83), Auto-EMME M=4.06 (SD 0.83). Expertise vs score r=0.58 in control, not significant in EMME groups. Backward jumps r=-0.52, pauses r=-0.41 with score.
limits: Lab study, undergraduates, one physiological trigger. Very large effects need replication.
agent_relevance: Help should be pulled when the agent is stuck, not pushed by a crude timer signal.

source: Padurean et al. (2026) Student mistakes and debugging when solving natural-language programming tasks
finding: In 900+ CS1 students writing prompts for code AI, the most common mistake was omitting key details. After failure students clarified intent more than they traced code or read tests.
numbers: Course of 1,031 enrolled; batch 1 N=887, batch 2 N=876 completed. Six Prompt Problems. Students rated prompting easier and more enjoyable than coding.
limits: Self-reported strategies, one course, one semester.
agent_relevance: Rewording is the weak repair move; tracing and testing is the strong one. Put a tracing step into repair.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2024) CodeAid: classroom deployment of an LLM programming assistant
finding: In a 12-week course with about 700 students, debugging features were the weakest. Help Fix Code was correct 63 percent and helpful 42 percent. Explain Code was 95 percent correct.
numbers: 563 research participants. Overall correct 79 percent, helpful 86 percent of correct (1,749 samples). General Question 91 percent correct. Question from Code 66 percent correct, 55 percent helpful, rating 3.28. Help Fix Code 63 percent correct (n=340), rating 2.67 of 5. Help Write Code 92 percent correct.
limits: Thematic coding of samples; one C systems course; Help Fix Code design changed mid-course.
agent_relevance: Debugging help is the hardest for LLMs. Fix proposals need verification.

source: Denny et al. (2022) Conversing with Copilot: prompt engineering for CS1 problems
finding: Copilot solved about half of 166 CS1 problems on the first try. Natural-language rewording of the problem fixed most of the rest.
numbers: 166 CodeCheck Python problems, July 2022. 79 solved first try (47.6 percent). 87 unsolved; 53 solved after rewording (about 60 percent). 15 unsolved problems were tagged Conceptual; 4 had ambiguous prompts.
limits: One model version, one problem set, authors wrote the rewordings.
agent_relevance: Failures often trace to a missing concept or ambiguous statement. Restating the problem is a real repair move.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2024) CodeAid: instructor view
finding: Educators worried about incorrect responses, especially for students with weak fundamentals, and wanted course-specific assistants.
numbers: Instructor interviews after seeing correctness data (79 percent overall, 63 percent for Help Fix Code).
limits: Few educators; opinion data.
agent_relevance: Wrong help hurts weak novices most, so verification matters most when the user cannot judge.

source: Prather et al. (2024) widening gap: new metacognitive difficulties
finding: GenAI added new metacognitive difficulties on top of five known ones from a prior 31-student study. Only 1 student had a new label without an old one.
numbers: Nine students tagged with old difficulties, eight with new ones. Struggling students thought they did better than they did.
limits: Qualitative tagging, N=21.
agent_relevance: Log a prediction of success before testing, then compare, to catch a false sense of progress.

source: Liffiton et al. (2023) CodeHelp: LLMs with guardrails for scalable support
finding: A guardrailed LLM help tool in a first-year course was valued for availability and error help. Instructors found it complemented staff.
numbers: 52 students over 12 weeks.
limits: I read the abstract and intro only, not the results tables.
agent_relevance: Guardrails against giving the answer need separate checks, since Hellas found LLMs ignore such instructions.

source: Golrang et al. (2026) EMME engagement behaviours
finding: Switching between the example video and the task predicted better debugging; backward jumps and pauses predicted worse. Auto-triggered help produced more of the bad pattern.
numbers: Task-video transitions r=0.32 (p=0.002). Transition counts differed by condition F(2,87)=4.95, p=0.009. Prior-expertise effect reduced in T-EMME (beta=-0.40, p=0.006) and Auto-EMME (beta=-0.48, p=0.007), L-EMME beta=-0.22, p=0.10.
limits: Correlational within conditions; N=120.
agent_relevance: Alternate between reading the model example and testing own code. Interleaving beats passive re-reading.

source: Padurean et al. (2026) prompt failure recovery
finding: Novices' common failure was leaving out details the AI could not guess, plus over-reliance on the AI to infer them.
numbers: More than 900 students, six dialogue-based Prompt Problems; 1,031 enrolled in the course.
limits: Mistake coding by three researchers; strategies self-reported.
agent_relevance: State all constraints explicitly in the problem restatement; do not rely on the reader to infer them.
